{
  "findings": [
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go",
      "line": 77,
      "severity": "high",
      "category": "perf",
      "title": "Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation",
      "body": "This change makes the entire background cleanup loop run every minute instead of every 10 minutes. It affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotation cleanup, and is not described in the PR. This can significantly increase database and filesystem load, and if a cleanup pass takes longer than one minute, queued ticks can cause passes to run back-to-back. Unless this is intentional, it should be reverted or made configurable."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 534,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "perf",
      "title": "Normal cleanup paths log at Error level and dump full ID lists",
      "body": "The new cleanup code calls Error-level logging on every successful batch, including batches that find zero rows, and includes the full ids slice in the log entry. Because batch sizes can be large, this can produce very large log lines and constant error-level noise during normal operation. These logs should be Debug or Info, and should likely log only counts or truncated IDs. Similar logging occurs later in the same file for count-based annotation cleanup and tag cleanup."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 611,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "perf",
      "title": "SQLite inline ID list is built with repeated Sprintf, causing O(n^2) copying",
      "body": "In the SQLite branch, the IN-list is constructed by repeatedly appending to the previous string with fmt.Sprintf. For large batches this repeatedly copies a growing string and becomes O(n^2) in the number of IDs. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands, this can cause noticeable CPU and memory overhead. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join instead."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 615,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "Only SQLite is protected against parameter limits",
      "body": "For non-SQLite databases, deleteByIDs builds a single DELETE ... WHERE id IN clause with one placeholder per ID. The code special-cases SQLite's parameter limit but does not chunk or otherwise protect other databases from driver or database placeholder limits. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured very large, the generated statement may exceed those limits and fail. Consider chunking deletes by a safe limit for all supported databases or validating the batch size."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 556,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "concurrency",
      "title": "Fetch-then-delete can delete annotations that are no longer excess for max-count cleanup",
      "body": "The max-count cleanup first selects IDs to delete and then deletes them in a separate statement. If newer annotations are deleted between the SELECT and DELETE, the selected older IDs may move inside the retained MaxCount set, so the job can delete annotations that would now be among the newest retained rows. If this best-effort behavior is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise the deletion needs a stronger consistency check."
    }
  ]
}

findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation
findings.body: This change makes the entire background cleanup loop run every minute instead of every 10 minutes. It affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotation cleanup, and is not described in the PR. This can significantly increase database and filesystem load, and if a cleanup pass takes longer than one minute, queued ticks can cause passes to run back-to-back. Unless this is intentional, it should be reverted or made configurable.

findings.title: Normal cleanup paths log at Error level and dump full ID lists
findings.body: The new cleanup code calls Error-level logging on every successful batch, including batches that find zero rows, and includes the full ids slice in the log entry. Because batch sizes can be large, this can produce very large log lines and constant error-level noise during normal operation. These logs should be Debug or Info, and should likely log only counts or truncated IDs. Similar logging occurs later in the same file for count-based annotation cleanup and tag cleanup.

findings.title: SQLite inline ID list is built with repeated Sprintf, causing O(n^2) copying
findings.body: In the SQLite branch, the IN-list is constructed by repeatedly appending to the previous string with fmt.Sprintf. For large batches this repeatedly copies a growing string and becomes O(n^2) in the number of IDs. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands, this can cause noticeable CPU and memory overhead. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

findings.title: Only SQLite is protected against parameter limits
findings.body: For non-SQLite databases, deleteByIDs builds a single DELETE ... WHERE id IN clause with one placeholder per ID. The code special-cases SQLite's parameter limit but does not chunk or otherwise protect other databases from driver or database placeholder limits. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured very large, the generated statement may exceed those limits and fail. Consider chunking deletes by a safe limit for all supported databases or validating the batch size.

findings.title: Fetch-then-delete can delete annotations that are no longer excess for max-count cleanup
findings.body: The max-count cleanup first selects IDs to delete and then deletes them in a separate statement. If newer annotations are deleted between the SELECT and DELETE, the selected older IDs may move inside the retained MaxCount set, so the job can delete annotations that would now be among the newest retained rows. If this best-effort behavior is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise the deletion needs a stronger consistency check.
